page: Vultr vhf-12c-48gb is a virtual server belonging to the High Frequency Compute family. It features an Intel x86_64 processor configured with 12 shared vCPUs, derived from 6 physical cores with hyper-threading enabled. The system is equipped with 48.0 GB of system memory, translating to 4.0 GB per core, and includes 768 GB of local NVMe SSD storage. It does not include dedicated GPU hardware.

Performance benchmarks indicate average to strong capabilities. Single-core and multi-core stress-ng tests place the server in the average tier, while single-threaded gzip compression performs in the top tier at 41.11 GB/sec. Memory performance is highly polarized: small-block cached read bandwidth is exceptionally high at 865.54 GB/sec, whereas large-block uncached read and write bandwidths fall into the weak tier at 33.97 GB/sec and 18.41 GB/sec, respectively. Passmark memory testing registers a top-tier score of 3149.22.

Given the shared CPU allocation and the contrast between high cached memory speeds and lower uncached throughput, this server is best suited for workloads with high locality of reference. It is appropriate for static web serving, intermediate database operations, and lightweight text processing or small-scale LLM inference. The bundled 768 GB NVMe SSD provides a solid storage foundation for data-intensive tasks, though the shared CPU model presents a tradeoff for sustained, high-compute workloads.
description: Vultr vhf-12c-48gb is an x86_64 virtual server in the High Frequency Compute family, featuring 12 shared Intel vCPUs and 48.0 GB of RAM. The configuration includes a bundled 768 GB NVMe SSD and one public IPv4 address, with no GPU acceleration. Benchmarks show top-tier performance in cached memory bandwidth and single-threaded gzip compression, though uncached large-block memory operations are relatively weak. With a balanced 1:4 vCPU-to-RAM ratio, this server is qualitatively cost-efficient for general-purpose workloads that benefit from fast local storage and high cache hit rates. It is well-suited for static web serving, database operations, and lightweight serialization tasks, though the shared CPU allocation may limit performance consistency under sustained, heavy compute loads.
